coredata.dc:description: In this study, bio-based β-farnesene (Far) and modified anionic cassava starch (ACS) were chosen as renewable alternatives to replace traditional non-renewable monomers in emulsifier-free emulsion polymerization for the development of bio-based materials. Graft copolymerization of Far and n-butyl acrylate (BA) onto ACS was carried out in a semi-batch emulsion polymerization, using 7.0 wt% of ACS and varying Far/BA ratios (100:0, 80:20, 70:30, 60:40, 50:50 and 0:100 wt%). By adjusting the Far/BA ratio, the final properties of the polymer latexes were effectively modulated. The use of ACS modified in situ proved colloidal stability of the latexes, with hydrodynamic diameter ranging from 150 to 200 nm and overall monomer conversion of 90–99 % for formulations containing up to 50 wt% Far. The gel content of poly(Far-co-BA)-g-ACS was significantly higher, while elongation at break decreased with increasing Far content. The glass transition temperature (Tg) of poly(Far-co-BA)-g-ACS ranged from −34 to +3.2 °C, which makes them attractive for a wide range of adhesive applications. The final polymers exhibited distinct adhesive performances, providing a strategic approach to tailoring end-use properties for specific applications. Furthermore, the use of in situ modified anionic cassava starch (ACS) provides valuable insights for the development of bio-based polymer materials under industrially relevant conditions.

ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: In this study, bio-based β-farnesene (Far) and modified anionic cassava starch (ACS) were chosen as renewable alternatives to replace traditional non-renewable monomers in emulsifier-free emulsion polymerization for the development of bio-based materials. Graft copolymerization of Far and n-butyl acrylate (BA) onto ACS was carried out in a semi-batch emulsion polymerization, using 7.0 wt% of ACS and varying Far/BA ratios (100:0, 80:20, 70:30, 60:40, 50:50 and 0:100 wt%). By adjusting the Far/BA ratio, the final properties of the polymer latexes were effectively modulated. The use of ACS modified in situ proved colloidal stability of the latexes, with hydrodynamic diameter ranging from 150 to 200 nm and overall monomer conversion of 90–99 % for formulations containing up to 50 wt% Far. The gel content of poly(Far-co-BA)-g-ACS was significantly higher, while elongation at break decreased with increasing Far content. The glass transition temperature (Tg) of poly(Far-co-BA)-g-ACS ranged from −34 to +3.2 °C, which makes them attractive for a wide range of adhesive applications. The final polymers exhibited distinct adhesive performances, providing a strategic approach to tailoring end-use properties for specific applications. Furthermore, the use of in situ modified anionic cassava starch (ACS) provides valuable insights for the development of bio-based polymer materials under industrially relevant conditions.

ce:section.ce:para: The development of bio-based polymer dispersions from renewable sources has gained significant attention in recent years due to growing environmental concerns to replace nonrenewable petroleum-based monomers, such as 1,3-butadiene and isoprene, avoiding the use of expensive pressurized reactors for a broad range of industrial applications, including paper coatings, elastomers, adhesives, and others (Behr & Johnen, 2009; Droesbeke et al., 2020; Luk & Maric, 2019, 2021; Rigo et al., 2023; Rodrigues & Oliveira, 2024; Sahu et al., 2023; Sahu & Oh, 2022). The global production of bio-based polymer latexes and the use of bio-based materials in the latex formulation reflect in the reduction of the synthetic polymer content where possible and further increase sustainability (Mohebbi et al., 2025).

The use of modified cassava starch in water-based polymer dispersions as an alternative to traditional surfactants and nonrenewable monomers has gained more attention due to its low cost, biodegradability, availability, and renewability (Cazotti et al., 2020; Rigo et al., 2023; Rodrigues & Oliveira, 2024). Starch, one of the most abundant polysaccharides present in plants, consists primarily of two major components: amylose and amylopectin. Amylose is composed of linear chains of glucose units linked by (α)-1,4-glycosidic bonds, while amylopectin consists of branched chains of glucose units linked by α-1,4-glycosidic bonds (Rashwan et al., 2024; Zeeman et al., 2015). Starch can be sourced on a large scale from various plants, including rice, sorghum, potatoes, cassava, and corn (Zeeman et al., 2015). Starch from potatoes, corn, and cassava typically has an amylose content ranging from 20 to 30 % in regular varieties, with high-amylose varieties containing up to 80 %. Cassava roots are a crop in many tropical regions and typically contain high starch content (60 % to 80 % by dry weight), predominantly composed of amylopectin (Rashwan et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2022). Therefore, modified starch is a suitable candidate for an eco-friendly replacement of petroleum-based polymer dispersions.

Graft copolymerization of starch is a crucial approach to enhance the physicochemical properties of starch and can be achieved via grafting from, grafting to, or grafting through approaches (Cazotti et al., 2020; Meimoun et al., 2018; Rodrigues et al., 2021; Smeets et al., 2017). Furthermore, various drawbacks were still present, such as latex instability, water absorption, production cost, and low reactivity ratios when bio-based monomers are used. The cassava starch used in the present work is a modified anionic starch which represent the same industrial operation conditions for latex production. Typically, the industrial procedure is divided into two main steps: the cleavage of starch into oligosaccharides units, followed by graft polymerization with the desired monomer and initiator (Meimoun et al., 2018). In this sense, cassava starch hydrolysis can be performed in situ within the same reactor where the subsequent polymerization takes place. Latex polymer particles stabilized by in situ modified starch have previously been obtained by generating free radicals on the starch backbone through a redox initiation system, allowing it to react with a range of traditional monomers (Möller & Glittenberg, 1990; Brune & Von Eben-Worlée, 2002; Cho & Lee, 2002; Meshram et al., 2009; Gaborieau et al., 2009; Krückel & Werner, 2011; Cheng et al., 2014, 2018; Rodrigues et al., 2020, Rodrigues et al., 2021; Worzakowska, 2023). On the other hand, the graft polymerization of the bio-based monomers, such as β-farnesene, has not been thoroughly investigated.

The main challenges in producing latexes with β-farnesene (Far) via emulsifier-free emulsion polymerization include low monomer conversion, low water solubility, low molar mass, limited colloidal stability, and insufficient end-use properties required for effective polymer latex applications (Rigo et al., 2023; Rodrigues & Oliveira, 2024; Sahu et al., 2023). In this sense, Far a bio-based acyclic sesquiterpene produced on a large scale in Brazil through sucrose fermentation (Benjamin et al., 2016; Sahu et al., 2023; Sahu & Bhowmick, 2019) is a good alternative. Fig. 1 shows the schematic illustration and chemical structure of Far obtained from Brazilian sugar cane with engineered yeast (Sahu & Oh, 2022., Sahu et al., 2023). The conjugated double bonds in their structures enable them to undergo polymerization and cross-linked using conventional industrial reactions commonly used in the production of adhesives and elastomers (Nelson et al., 2022; Sahu et al., 2023; Rodrigues & Oliveira, 2024). According to Sahu and Oh (2022) and Sahu et al. (2023) the polymerization of Far occurs predominantly in the double bond between 1,4-cis and 1,4-trans.

However, various drawbacks were still present in the use of the bio-based Far via emulsifier-free emulsion polymerization technique, such as high hydrophobicity and low reactivity ratios of Far monomer, resulting in polymers with low overall monomer conversion and low molar mass because they are not adapted to radical polymerization in aqueous dispersed media (Rigo et al., 2023). Sahu and Bhowmick (2019) described the redox polymerization of Far at room temperature, resulting in a very low monomer conversion (20 to 24 %) and polymer with low molar mass after 24 h of polymerization. Sahu and Oh (2022) and Sahu et al. (2023) reported monomer conversion around 80 % in the emulsion polymerization of Far and Far/styrene with 12 h of polymerization at 70 °C. Luk and Maric (2021) also reported low monomer conversion (30 and 40 %) in the miniemulsion polymerization of Far. Therefore, challenges remain in optimizing the synthesis and properties of the bio-based polymer dispersion to meet specific production and application requirements of industrial production.

Recently, we have reported the emulsion copolymerization of Far and BA using anionic surfactant and ammonium persulfate for pressure sensitive adhesives (Rodrigues & Oliveira, 2024). Worzakowska (2019) presented studies on the optimization of the free-radical graft polymerization of terpene acrylate monomers prepared from two geometric isomers of terpene alcohol, such as trans-3,7-dimethyl-2,6-octadien-1-ol and cis-3,7-dimethyl-2,6-octadien-1-ol with potato starch. In this sense, the use of enzymatic hydrolysis and peroxide treatment of starch in situ involves the breakdown of starch molecules into smaller units and starch radicals before polymerization of Far and BA monomers, leading to the formation of amphiphilic oligomers and subsequent polymer particles, which stabilize the latex particles by branched oligosaccharides (Gaborieau et al., 2009; Rodrigues et al., 2020).

The combination of Far and BA with hydrolyzed starch presents an interesting strategy to improve the monomer conversion of Far through copolymerization with BA. In-situ starch degradation using α-amylase and peroxide, followed by the addition of ammonium persulfate during polymerization, enhances the generation rate of oligomeric radicals in the aqueous phase, and this strategy is critical for overcoming the associated challenges. Furthermore, the use of starch as a component in copolymer poly(BA-co-Far)-g-starch for adhesives enhances cohesive and mechanical properties, which are essential for applications requiring high shear strength and mechanical properties (Rodrigues & Oliveira, 2024). In addition, the graft copolymerization of starch with BA can improve the thermal stability, mechanical strength, and colloidal stability without the need for conventional surfactants, making it more suitable for adhesive applications (Monroy et al., 2023; Rodrigues et al., 2021; Rodrigues & Oliveira, 2024).

Given the technological importance of Far and anionic cassava starch, this study investigates the graft copolymerization of Far with BA using in situ modified ACS as a stabilizer. The polymerizations were carried out via emulsifier-free emulsion polymerization under industrial operating conditions to synthesize poly(Far-co-BA)-g-starch for adhesive applications. This technique is commonly used in industrial latex production in order to obtain polymer dispersions. However, in this study the effect of different Far/BA ratios were examined in terms of monomer conversion, hydrodynamic diameter, colloidal stability, thermal, mechanical, and end-use properties. The consequent effects of Far/BA contents were evaluated in terms of chemical structures by FTIR, 13C NMR and Tg. Additionally, the adhesive performance of the latex films was evaluated based on tack, peel strength, and shear strength.

Technical grade monomers, trans-β-farnesene (Far, ≥ 97 %), known as Biofene® and n-butyl acrylate (BA, ≥ 98 %) were kindly provided by Amyris Biotechnol and BASF SA, respectively. The monomers were purified twice through a column of activated aluminum oxide (Al2O3, Brockmann, Type 1, 150 mesh, Millipore Sigma) to remove any traces of inhibitors and impurities, dried using a molecular sieve (3 Å, Millipore Sigma), and then stored at −2 °C before use. Ammonium persulfate (APS, ≥98 %) was purchased from BASF SA, purified by recrystallization, and dried under vacuum at 30 °C before use. Hydrogen peroxide (HPO, 35 %, Acros Organics), and formaldehyde-free reducing agent (2-hydroxy-2-sulfinatoacetic acid disodium salt, Bruggolite® FF6 M, Brüggemann Chemical) were used as received. Anionic cassava starch (ACS, Superion® 3050), with a degree of substitution (DS) of 0.040 molmol and an amylopectin content of 76 % (Table S1, Supplementary Information), was supplied by Horizonte Amidos Ltda., purified by washing twice with ethanol, and then was dried in an oven at 50 °C for 48 h prior to use. Thermostable α-amylase enzyme (α-1,4-glucan-4-glucanohydrolase) from Bacillus amyloliquefaciens with an activity of 120 KNU-B/g (Aquazym® 120 L) was obtained from Novozymes Latin America Ltd. (Brazil) and stored at 5 °C before use. Ethanol (≥ 99.8 %) and calcium acetate (≥ 99.8 %) were obtained from Lab. Synth and used as received. N,N-dimethylformamide HPLC grade (DMF, >99.9 %) and lithium bromide (≥ 99 %) were obtained from Millipore-Sigma. Spectra/Por® dialysis membrane with MWCO of 14,000 kDa was purchased from Spectrum Labs. Biaxially oriented polypropylene (BOPP) film with surface energy of 45 dynas cm−1 were obtained from Arconvert Brazil and used to prepare the adhesive tapes. Deionized water (DW) with a conductivity of 2.1 μS/cm was used throughout the study.

Starch graft polymerizations were carried out via emulsifier-free emulsion polymerization, using ACS as a stabilizer and different Far/BA ratios in a 0.6 L jacketed glass reactor equipped with a reflux condenser, stainless steel anchor-shape stirrer, water bath, dosing pump system and nitrogen purging tube. Table 1 shows the Far/BA ratios used to prepare the latexes. All polymerizations were done through a semi-batch process using 7.0 wt% of ACS (relative to total latex mass) in a two-step procedure (Rodrigues et al., 2020, 2021). In the first step, the reactor was loaded with ACS (35 g), deionized water (221.15 g), calcium acetate (0.10 g), and α-amylase (0.25 g). The mixture was heated up to 85 °C under continuous stirring at 180 rpm and then was kept for 5 min. After, a solution of 2-hydroxy-2-sulfinatoacetic acid disodium salt (FF6 M) (1.2 g) was prepared in deionized water (5.0 g) and then added dropwise in the reactor, followed by addition of HPO solution (0.7 g) in deionized water (10 g) over a period of 10 min, using a dropping funnel. In the second step, the monomer mixture (Far/BA) and APS solution (80.0 g) at a concentration of 6.3 wt% in deionized water were added dropwise into reactor at a controlled feed rate over a period of 3 and 4.5 h, respectively. During all experiments, the temperature of the reactor was maintained at (85 ± 1) °C. Finally, the latexes (35.7 % solids content) were then cooled to 30 °C, filtered through a 300 μm nylon bag, and then characterized. Coagulum content was determined gravimetrically. The latex (100 g) was diluted with deionized water (300 g), filtered through a stainless-steel screen (125 μm) and then dried in an air-circulation oven for 1 h at 120 °C. After drying, the retained polymer was weighed, and the amount of coagulum was determined (Oliveira, 2010, Santos et al., 2024). The latexes were purified by dialysis using a semi-permeable dialysis membrane (MWCO of 12–14.0 kDa, Sectra/Por® 2) under magnetic stirring for 7 days at 25 °C to remove non-grafted ACS, oligomers, and impurities. Approximately 100 g of each latex was placed in rinsed dialysis tubing (0.32 mL/cm) and dialyzed against deionized water (pH = 7.5) for one week. During this period, the water (1.5 l) was replaced twice daily until electrical conductivity stabilized. The cleaned latexes were then used for the preparation of polymeric films and subsequent characterizations.

The viscosity of the latexes was evaluated using a Brookfield LVF viscometer (Spindle 6, 60 rpm) at 25 °C. The solid content (SC) of the latexes was determined gravimetrically. The collected samples from the reactor were stopped using a hydroquinone solution combined with an ice-water bath. Approximately 1.0 g of each sample was weighed into aluminum pans and dried in a ventilated oven at 140 °C for 1 h. Each analysis was performed in triplicate, and the average values were reported. The final overall monomer conversion (Xg) was determined from the solids content, using Eq. 1. (Oliveira et al., 2011).

The average hydrodynamic diameter (HD) and hydrodynamic diameter distribution (HDÐ) of the latexes were determined by dynamic light scattering (DLS) using the Beckman Coulter Delsa Nano C instrument at 25 °C. The original and purified latex samples (1 mL) were diluted with deionized water (100 mL), placed into a cuvette, and then analyzed at an angle of 165°. The latex samples were also evaluated after storage in an oven at 60 °C for 72 h and after six months at 25 °C. This procedure was repeated three times with a new sample, and the average values were determined using the Stokes-Einstein equation. Electrophoretic mobility (ζ-potential) was measured using a Delsa Nano C instrument, calibrated with a 0.1 M NaCl solution. The latex samples were diluted in water and measured at 25 °C. For each analysis, three replicate samples were used and the average values were reported. All samples were also evaluated after six months of storage at 25 °C. The pH of the latexes was determined using an Orion model 310 digital pH meter at 25 °C (Rodrigues et al., 2020).

Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) measurements of the latex films were conducted on a Perkin Elmer Spectrum II spectrometer using an Attenuated Total Reflectance (ATR) accessory with a total of 32 scans in the frequency range 4000–400 cm−1 and resolution of 4 cm−1.

The presence of the grafted ACS in the copolymers was evaluated by solid-state 13C NMR analysis using a Varian VNMRS 400 spectrometer, operating at a field frequency of 400 MHz and 16 scans at 30 °C. All analyses were carried out following the purification of the latex.

The gel content (GC) of the polymer samples with different Far/BA ratios was determined in duplicate using the Soxhlet extraction method with DMF as the solvent. Initially, the latexes were purified by dialysis, placed in silicone molds at (25 ± 2) oC and (50 ± 5) % of relative humidity (RH) for 7 days and then were dried in a vacuum oven at (40 ± 2) °C for 24 h. The samples were weighed in a cellulose filter cartridge and placed in a Soxhlet extractor with DMF (300 mL), followed by refluxing for 20 h. Thereafter, the cellulose cartridge was removed and dried in a vacuum oven at 60 °C until a constant weight was reached (Rodrigues & Oliveira, 2024). The grafting efficiency (GE) was determined as the ratio between the grafted copolymer after Soxhlet extraction and the mass of monomer charged (Cheng et al., 2018; Meimoun et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2017).

Polymer samples were dried under vacuum at 40 °C for 24 h prior to differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and thermogravimetric (TGA) analysis. The glass transition temperature (Tg) was determined on a TA Instruments Q2000 analyzer under a nitrogen flow rate of 50 mL min−1. Approximately 8.0 mg of each polymer sample was enclosed in an aluminum hermetic pan, cooled to −90 °C, held isothermally for 2 min, and heated to 70 °C with two cycles of cooling and heating at a heating/cooling rate of 10 °C min−1. The Tg values were obtained from the second heating run. TGA analysis was performed on a TA Instruments Q500 analyzer in a nitrogen flow rate of 50 mL min−1. Approximately 8.0 mg of each purified sample was placed in a platinum pan and heated from 30 to 500 °C at a rate of 10 °C min−1, following the procedure described by Rodrigues et al. (2021).

The tensile properties of the latex films were evaluated using a tensile testing machine (EMIC DL-2000) in accordance with ASTM D638-14 standard at a testing speed at 50 mm min−1 (American Society for Testing and Materials (ASTM), 2014). Latexes films were prepared by casting into a silicone mold and dried under controlled conditions of (25 ± 2) oC and (50 ± 5) % RH for 7 days, followed by storage in a vacuum oven at 40 °C for 12 h prior analysis. Seven specimens from each latex film were evaluated and the average values were reported (Rodrigues et al., 2021; Romão et al., 2022). Pendulum hardness was measured using a König pendulum hardness tester (BYK Gardner GmbH) in accordance with ASTM D4366-16 (American Society for Testing and Materials (ASTM), 2016). The films with thickness of 300 μm were produced from the latexes by casting on glass plates and dried at (100 ± 2) oC for 10 min in an air-circulating oven and then was cooled for 30 min at (25 ± 2) oC and (50 ± 5)% RH (Santos et al., 2024).

Adhesive tapes were prepared on corona-treated BOPP films (21× 30) cm. Latex samples were coated onto BOPP films using a coater machine equipped with a regulating ruler and then dried in an air-circulation oven at 100 °C for 3 min. The amount of polymer latex coated onto the BOPP films was 20.0 g m−2 based on dry latex. After drying, the BOPP films were attached to release paper, cut into strips of (100 × 25) mm, and then conditioned at (23 ± 2) °C and (50 ± 5) % RH for 7 days (Mateus, 2017; Rodrigues & Oliveira, 2024). The force required to remove the adhesive tape (30 × 25) mm into contact with stainless steel plates was measured according to the FINAT standard methods (FTM 1 and 9) at (23 ± 2) °C and (50 ± 5) % RH. A Universal tester machine (Katos Instrument) at 300 mm min−1 and an area of 25 mm2 was used. The maximum force recorded by the equipment after the minimum contact time between the tape and the substrate was reported as loop tack in N/25 mm. The adhesive tapes (30 × 25) mm were laminated against stainless steel to make a contact area of 25 mm2 and then the steel plates with the adhesive tape were suspended with 1 kg of weight at the free end of the specimen, according to the FINAT standard methods (FTM 8). The time to shear failure from the stainless steel was recorded as shear resistance, and the average of eight samples was reported (Mateus, 2017).

In this study, anionic cassava starch (ACS) was modified in situ using α-amylase enzyme and a redox system (HPO/2-hydroxy-2-sulfinatoacetic acid disodium salt) to facilitate the grafting reactions with different Far/BA ratios. The use of an α-amylase and redox system in the first step effectively cleaved the starch into oligosaccharides and generated starch fragment radicals (ACS*) via hydrogen abstraction. The use of APS in the second step, followed by the gradual addition of the monomer mixture (Far/BA) under starved-feed conditions, ensures sufficient free radical generation during emulsifier -free emulsion polymerization.

Fig. 4 shows the overall monomer conversion and hydrodynamic diameter of the latexes with different Far/BA contents. The overall monomer conversion gradually decreased with increasing the amount of Far. Nevertheless, the hydrodynamic diameter slightly decreases from 205 nm (Run Far0) to 155 nm (Run Far10) by the introduction of Far from 0 to 10 wt% and remains practically constant by the introduction of Far up to 50 %, indicating the homogeneity of the latexes with Far and BA (Table 2). Furthermore, the HDÐ of all latexes were between 0.15 and 0.08 and the coagulum content gradually increased with the Far content increase. The low stability of the latex without BA (Run Far100) can be attributed to the absence of amphiphilic poly(BA)-g-starch in the continuous phase, resulting in low monomer conversion (32 %), low particle nucleation, higher monomer droplets and inhibition effect due to poor interaction between Far droplets and oligosaccharides radicals.

The obtained values are consistent with previous studies on Far polymerization using emulsion polymerization and conventional anionic surfactant (Rodrigues & Oliveira, 2024; Sahu & Bhowmick, 2019; Sahu & Oh, 2022. Sahu and Oh (2022) reported poly(Far) latex with an average particle diameter around 111.0 nm using sodium dodecyl sulfate as anionic surfactant. Rodrigues and Oliveira (2024) described latex of poly(Far-co-BA) with an average hydrodynamic diameter ranging from 120 to 130 nm and narrow HDÐ when anionic surfactant (Dowfax 2A1) was used. Considering that the molar mass of ACS decreased from 3.0 × 105 g mol−1 to 2.93 × 104 g mol−1 after enzymatic and redox treatment, the reduction in overall conversion can be associated with the low reactivity of Far with BA, due to the high steric hindrance of Far (Sahu et al., 2023; Sahu & Oh, 2022; Sarkar & Bhowmick, 2016). The low water solubilities of Far (< 0.0001 g L−1) and lower transport of the monomer to the growing particles, decrease the efficiency of particle nucleation (Rodrigues & Oliveira, 2024). Sahu and Bhowmick (2019) reported low monomer conversion (∼20 %) for poly(Far) obtained via emulsion polymerization. Luk and Maric (2021) also reported low monomer conversion (30–40 %) for poly(Far) after 30 h of polymerization. Sahu and Oh (2022) and Sahu et al. (2023) also reported monomer conversion of 80 % and 28 % for poly(Far) after 16 h and 4 h of polymerization, respectively.

In this work, the polymerizations were carried out after the first step by initiator and monomer-starved feed conditions to control the graft polymerization. However, under monomer-starved conditions, the oligosaccharides macro-radicals formed in situ starting the polymerization of BA and subsequent formation of amphiphilic graft oligomers (Fig. 3). These graft oligomers self-assembled to form pseudo-micelles, which spontaneously form the polymer particles stabilized by branched oligosaccharides. Particle nucleation takes place when radicals formed in the aqueous phase grow via propagation and then enter the particles or pseudo-micelles. When the amount of BA increased, the formation of amphiphilic graft oligomers was enhanced, leading to improved grafting reactions and stable particles (Table 2). Schork and Back (2004) showed that for highly water-insoluble monomers, the low water solubility results in long residence times of the oligomers in the aqueous phase before they reach sufficient length to enter polymer particles. In that regard, the polymerization rate and the particle nucleation are highly dependent on the water solubility and ability of the Far to diffuse into the continuous phase saturated with the monomer. However, in a copolymerization of Far/BA, the equilibrium monomer concentration of Far and BA in the aqueous phase should be depend on the content of BA in the monomer droplets (Schork, 2024). The overall monomer conversion data suggest good conversion of above 90 % until 50 wt% of Far. The low reactivity ratio of Far/BA (rBA < rFar) and the low water solubility of Far (< 0.0001 g L−1) help explain the tendency to form poly(BA)-g-starch. The absence of amphiphilic oligomers of poly(BA)-g-starch resulted in low monomer conversion, low colloidal stability and low hydrodynamic diameter for the polymerization of Far100.

The colloidal stability of the latexes was evaluated by measuring the zeta potential and hydrodynamic diameter before and after 6 months of storage (Table 2), as well as at different pH values (1.5, 6, and 10) (Fig. S4, supplementary information). The electrophoretic mobility of the final latexes did not change significantly with the addition of the Far monomer (Table 2), ranging from −34 to −42 mV. The negative ζ-potential is attributed to the anionic cassava starch and persulfate radicals which remained on the particle surface. Graft polymerizations performed with different Far/BA contents and 7.0 wt% of ACS did not exhibit significant differences with respect to the pH and viscosity of the final latex. To evaluate the effect of Far content on the colloidal stability of the latexes, hydrodynamic diameter was determined after 72 h at 60 °C in an oven, and after six months at 25 °C. Table 2 shows that all latexes displayed nearly diameter values before and after stability test, which indicates that they are completely stable. All the latexes with Far exhibit low hydrodynamic diameter ranging from 147 to 173 nm. On the other hand, the homopolymer poly(Far) (Run Far100) exhibited phase separation after the synthesis process (Fig. 2), reflecting poor colloidal stability in the absence of BA.

The stability of the latexes was also confirmed by ζ-potential measurements, as illustrated in Table 2, and indicating good colloidal stability over time. The latexes remained stable after six months of storage at 25 °C, even at low pH values (Table 2, Fig. S4). Additionally, the ζ-potential values exhibited a similar trend for all latexes after six months, suggesting that the differences in surface charge and hydrodynamic diameter are insufficient to cause significantly changes in colloidal stability (see Fig. S4 in Supplementary Information).

Fig. 5 (a,b) shows the effect of Far content on the visual aspect of the polymeric films before and after purification by dialysis. The polymer latex films without purification exhibited a brown coloration (Fig. 5a) due to the presence of residual impurities, while the purified latex exhibited a polymer film with a clear coloration (Fig. 5b), indicating the effective removal of residual components. Hydrogen peroxide, α-amylase enzyme and monomer-free can react, changing the coloration of the latex films. Additionally, oxidative curing of the free-double bonds in the poly(Far-co-BA) can occur, modifying the coloration of the latex film. Similar results were reported by Smeets et al. (2017), Rodrigues et al. (2021), and Rodrigues and Oliveira (2024). Dialysis efficiently removes free cassava starch, oligomers, free-oligosaccharides and free-monomers, thereby improving the purity of the latex film (Gaborieau et al., 2009). The brown coloration of the latex films can be attributed to the presence of free double bonds in the poly(Far) backbone and fragments of cassava starch in the water phase at pH = 1.5, which can cause degradation and oxidation (Asempour et al., 2024; Cheng et al., 2018; Giacomini & Ticianelli, 1999; Luk & Maric, 2021; Meshram et al., 2009; Rodrigues & Oliveira, 2024).

Fig. 6 shows the FTIR spectrum of poly(BA) (Run Far0) and poly(BA-co-Far)-g-ACS films (Runs Far10 – Far50), indicating the consumption of both Far and BA. The broad and intense peak at around 3100–3500 cm−1 is assigned to the stretching vibration of OH groups of ACS and the peaks at 1440, 1140 and 1017 cm−1 are attributed to the stretching vibrations of the glucose units (Cheng et al., 2018; Meshram et al., 2009; Rodrigues et al., 2020). The small peak at 3088 cm−1 corresponds to the C − H stretching of the conjugated double bond of Far, which disappears after polymerization (Sahu & Oh, 2022). The broad peak at around 2970, 2920 and 2855 cm−1 are attributed to the −CH3, −CH2, and − CH asymmetric stretching vibration of poly(BA-co-Far), respectively. The absorption band at 1735–1750 cm−1 is assigned to the ester group (O-C=O) from BA and suggests that a certain amount of BA was grafted onto ACS (Rodrigues et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2017). The sharp decrease in the intensities of the peaks at 990 and 890 cm−1 from Far indicates the use of unsaturated conjugated double bonds (Sahu et al., 2023; Sahu & Oh, 2022). The appearance of the new peaks at 1660 cm−1 into poly(BA-co-Far)-g-ACS and absent into poly(BA) (Run Far0), is attributed to the presence of isolated C7 C8 and C12 C13 double bond stretching in the structure (Sahu et al., 2023; Sahu & Oh, 2022), which provides substantial evidence that the BA and Far were grafted onto ACS backbone.

The gel content and molar mass of the soluble fraction for different Far and BA contents were determined, and the results are shown in Fig. 7 (a,b). The gel content increases, and the molar masses (
Mn ¯
and
Mw ¯
) decreases varying Far/BA ratio (Fig. 7b). The molar mass and gel content results showed significant changes in comparison with the polymer without Far (Run Far0), which can be associated with the amount of BA and Far grafted onto the ACS backbone, the crosslinked degree and solubility of the polymer in the solvent used. The polymer film without Far dissolved completely in DMF, showing no gel-like appearance. On the other hand, the polymer films containing different Far contents were insoluble in solvent DMF, suggesting strong intermolecular interactions or crosslinked structures that limit their solubility. In this work, the samples were subjected to a purification process, and it is expected that all non-grafted ACS was effectively removed. The decrease in molar masses and the increased gel content before and after latex purification suggest that Far led to crosslinking reactions. The highest molar mass values were obtained for the reference polymer (Run Far0), with
Mw ¯
= 1.2 × 105 g mol−1 and
Mn ¯
=5.0 × 104 g mol−1, whereas the polymer with 50 wt% of Far (Run Far50) exhibited the lowest molar mass values (∼1.0 × 104 g mol−1). Therefore, the molar masses of the graft polymers were affected by the presence of different contents of Far and grafting percentage.

The gel content values of the non-purified polymer films increased from 0 wt% to 57.8 wt%, while the purified films exhibited values between 0 % and 96 % (Fig. 7(a), confirming the high degree of crosslinking and low solubility in DMF. The replacement of BA by Far resulted in an increase in gel content, and the grafting efficiency values initially remained constant and decreased after 30 wt% of Far (Fig. 7b). The graft efficiency results are consistent with the schematic particle nucleation mechanism illustrated in Fig. 2, wherein the faster polymerization rate of BA compared to Far promotes greater grafting efficiency. After dialysis purification, oligomers and non-grafted ACS were removed, reducing the number of polymer chains available for dissolution in DMF and resulting in a decrease of the molar mass obtained by GPC (Fig. 7b) (Arzamendi & Leiza, 2008; Cheng & Zhao, 2017; Sahu et al., 2023). The increase in gel content with the increase in Far content was also observed by other authors (Rodrigues & Oliveira, 2024; Sahu et al., 2023). The gel content values after latex purification obtained in this study were higher than those reported for poly(Far-co-BA) with 20/80 wt% of Far/BA synthesized using alkyl diphenyl oxide disulfonate (Rodrigues & Oliveira, 2024), suggesting that the grafting of starch affects the gel content. Molina-Gutiérrez et al. (2020) reported a moderate increase in gel content with the increasing concentration of the ethoxy dihydroeugenyl methacrylate biobased monomer in the latex formulation.

The grafting efficiency was also determined by 13C NMR to investigate the presence of grafted polymers onto ACS. Fig. 8 (a,b) show the 13C NMR spectrum of poly(BA-co-Far)-g-ACS synthesized with 50 and 20 wt% Far, respectively. The solid-state resonance signals at 15.0, 16.6, and 24.6 ppm are assigned to the methyl carbons (C9, C14, and C15) in the Far backbone. The methylene carbons from Far appear at 25.6, 30.4, and 38.7 ppm, while the signals in the region of 112–147 ppm correspond to the carbon‑carbon double bonds present in Far (Sahu & Oh, 2022). In addition, the significant reduction in the intensity of carbon signals bonded to OH groups from ACS indicates that the grafting process of Far/BA onto the ACS backbone was efficient. These findings suggest successful grafting of the polymer onto ACS.

Fig. 9 (a,b) shows the thermal stability of pol(BA)-g-starch and poly(Far-co-BA)-g-starch films, performed by TGA analysis under nitrogen atmosphere to understand thermal decomposition and residual mass as a function of different Far/BA ratios. TGA results demonstrate that the presence of Far improves the residual mass but decreases the thermal stability of the poly(Far-co-BA)-g-starch, indicating differences in polymer composition, grafting efficiency and crosslinking reactions. According to curves showed in Fig. 9(a,b), two main stages of thermal degradation were obtained for the polymers. The first stage of decomposition located between 150 and 200 °C was due to water evaporation and decomposition of low molar mass species of hydrolyzed ACS (Rodrigues et al., 2020). According to corresponding TGA thermogram of ACS (Fig. S3, supplementary information), an initial mass loss of 6.26 % at 150 °C is attributed to adsorbed moisture and small fragments of ACS and the maximum degradation temperature (Tmax) at ∼293 °C, with mass loss of ∼55 %. Furthermore, the main decomposition of all polymer films occurred in the second stage between 300 and 400 °C, with similar residual mass for all polymer films, except for the Far30 and Far50 with 9.3 % of residual mass, due the formation of crosslinked structure above 400 °C.

The maximum degradation temperature for all polymer was approximately 400 °C, indicating the effect of BA and Far content on the thermal properties of the polymers. These results suggests that the grafting efficiency of BA was higher than that of Far, leading to the formation of polymers rich in of poly(BA)-g-starch. The polymer films obtained with higher BA content exhibited enhanced thermal stability. During the second decomposition stage (∼350 °C), the mass loss of the polymer Far50 decreases from 19.0 % to ∼65.0 %, indicating that the addition of 50 wt% of Far is responsible to decrease the thermal stability of the polymer at 350 °C (Run Far50). These events can be associated to the thermal decomposition of pendant chain-end unsaturation in the polyFar moiety (Sahu et al., 2023; Sahu & Oh, 2022). Sahu et al. (2023) reported low thermal stability for poly(Far-co-styrene) with varying Far/styrene ratios. Orzolek et al. (2018), described that increasing the units of Far substitutions from 5 to 15 over 10 monomer units in starch-Far reduces the onset thermal decomposition temperature by approximately 9 °C.

The Tg of the polymer films with different Far/BA ratios was determined by differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), and compared with theoretical Tg values calculated using the Fox-Flory equation (Fox & Flory, 1950). The addition of Far resulted in a decrease in Tg, indicating that the degree of crosslinking and graphitization of Far onto ACS resulted in a modification of the polymer chain mobility (Fig. 10b). The presence of cross-links between chains restricts rotational motion, and thus cross-linking introduces restriction and stiffness in the polymer. The Tg values of poly(Far-co-BA)-g-ACS determined by DSC ranged from ∼3.2 °C to −34.0 °C, depending on the Far/BA ratios, while the Tg of poly(BA)-g-ACS (Run Far0) was around 7.4 °C. All the polymers exhibited slightly higher Tg values compared with theoretical ones (Fig. 10a), most probably due to some degree of crosslinking and the use of ACS, which has a higher Tg (∼55 °C).

The obtained Tg values are directly related to the structure of poly(Far), which consists of long aliphatic chains with multiple double bonds, providing greater flexibility and mobility to the polymer chains, resulting in a lower Tg value (Sahu et al., 2023). These results were comparable with our previous studies of poly(Far/BA) using surfactant (Rodrigues & Oliveira, 2024). When the polymerization of poly(BA) and poly(Far/BA) with 20 wt% of Far was carried out without ACS the Tg values was −55 °C and 10 °C, respectively (Rodrigues & Oliveira, 2024). This behavior also may be attributed to the covalent bonding of OH groups of ACS with Far and BA, resulting in changes the chain mobility of the polymers and polymer structure.

According to literature, the Tg of polyFar is −68 °C (Sahu & Oh, 2022) and the Tg of poly(BA) is around −55 °C (Rodrigues & Oliveira, 2024). Derivations from theoretical and experimental values may occur caused by interactions between the ACS-g-polymer, crosslinking reactions and free CCS in the water phase (Rodrigues et al., 2020). These results are consistent with those exhibited by the gel content (Fig. 7a) in this work. Sahu et al. (2023) reported an increase in Tg values with the increase in styrene contents for poly(Far-co-styrene) copolymers, ranging from −58.0 °C to −38.0 °C. This fact would explain a tendency to form poly(BA)-ACS and poly(Far-BA)-g-ACS richer in BA than in Far. The Tg values of starch-graft polymer with different starch content were shifted slightly higher as compared to the Tg of polymer obtained without starch (Cheng et al., 2014; Rodrigues et al., 2020).

The stress and elongation at break of the latex films varying Far/BA contents were evaluated using tensile testing before and after purification, as shown in Fig. 11 (a,b). The stress values of the latex films purified and non-purified increased initially (Run Far10) and decreased with increasing Far contents. When the amount of Far was increased from 0 wt% to 20 wt%, elongation at break decreased significantly, indicating the rigid and brittle properties of the polymeric film. The latex films up to a Far content of 20 wt% had lower elongation at break (380 % and 300 %), compared to the latex film without Far (750 %). On the other hand, the purified films exhibited significantly lower elongation values compared to the non-purified films (Fig. 11b). The higher stress observed in the purified films may be related to the removal of residual compounds, such as nongrafted starch and oligomers, leading to greater structural cohesion and, consequently, a more rigid structure. This justifies the slightly higher stress values observed for the purified films (Rodrigues et al., 2020). However, when 30 %, 40 % and 50 % of Far were used, the elongation at break values remained practically constant. This behavior may be attributed to the Far segments in the polymer backbone and cross-linking degree. These results can be associated with both, gel content (Fig. 7a), thermal stability (Fig. 9) and Tg values (Fig. 10).

The addition of Far initially decreases the pendulum hardness (Fig. 12 ) and elongation of the polymer films, before and after purification by dialysis, up to a Far content of 20 wt%. When the Far content increased from 20 wt% to 50 wt%, the elongation at break showed a slight decrease, whereas the hardness increased. This behavior is associated with the starch grafting efficiency and the presence of pendant chain-end unsaturation in the poly(Far-co-BA)-g-ACS. The hardness of the polymer films are significantly influenced by the grafting efficiency, the extent of crosslinking, and the presence of non-grafted starch in the water phase. These non-grafted fragments act as “fillers” within the polymer film, enhancing its hardness (Rodrigues et al., 2021). This behavior is consistent with the Tg values exhibited in Fig. 10, although it is contrary to our initial expectations.

To investigate the effect of Far/BA ratios on adhesive properties like tack, peel and shear strength tests, BOPP tapes were prepared and the results are summarized in Table 3 . The adhesive tapes exhibited zero tack values for all Far/BA contents, attributed to the presence of ACS. Peel strength is defined as the force required to peel away a strip of adhesives coated film from a substrate at a standard peel rate. In this study, peel strength values increased gradually with Far content and the maximum value was obtained with 30 wt% of Far (Run Far30). Shear strength values initially increased with Far content and then decreased at higher Far contents (Table 3). The maximum shear strength value was observed at 30 wt% Far and can be attributed to the cohesive strength, which is linked to the crosslinking degree of poly(Far-co-BA)-g-ACS, as indicated by gel content, molar mass (Fig. 7b), Tg values (Fig. 10) and hardness (Fig. 12). Given that starch has a relatively higher Tg (∼55 °C), lower tack and peel strength were obtained for poly(BA)-g-ACS due to the presence of grafted ACS and its higher Tg. However, slightly higher tack and peel values were expected for poly(BA-co-Far)-g-ACS due to the Tg of these polymers (Fig. 10a). The consistently low (zero) tack values suggest that graft copolymerization of Far onto ACS, occurs primarily on the surface of polymer particles or remains free in the aqueous phase (Watcharakitti et al., 2022). This behavior is expected, due to high gel content (Fig. 7a), which negatively affects the adhesive performance of the polymer films (Lee et al., 2017). The internal crosslinking, ACS graphitization or ACS free result in low adhesion, setting a limitation for pressure-sensitive adhesive applications.

In previous studies, the tack values of petroleum-based pressure sensitive adhesives without starch ranged from 2.0 to 5.0 N/25 mm (Benedek, 2005; Mateus, 2017). In contrast, the adhesives obtained in this study exhibited peel strength values between 0.1 and 0.5 N/25 mm, with tack forces significantly lower than those typically reported for commercial pressure sensitive adhesives. However, the successful synthesis of bio-based polymers using Far and ACS via emulsifier-free emulsion polymerization, with good colloidal stability, thermal, and mechanical properties, indicates that poly(BA-co-Far)-g-ACS holds potential for alternative adhesive applications. Furthermore, for tape applications, optimizing adhesive properties will be essential to achieve a suitable balance between adhesion and cohesion, which can be accomplished by adjusting the contents of Far/BA and ACS.

This study successfully demonstrated the graft copolymerization of Far/BA monomers onto anionic cassava starch (ACS) using different Far/BA contents and 7.0 wt% of ACS as a substitute for conventional petroleum-based latex. The grafting of Far/BA monomers onto anionic cassava starch using α-amylase enzyme and redox system in situ was efficient to create free radical grafting sites through hydrogen abstraction. The results demonstrate the successful production of polymer latex with different Far/BA ratios, incorporating up to 50 wt% of Far as a bio-based monomer. The addition of Far had a significant effect on colloidal stability, monomer conversion, Tg, hardness and thermal properties of the polymers.

The hydrodynamic diameter and colloidal stability were strongly dependent on the concentration of BA. When BA was used with Far, poly(Far-co-BA)-g-starch was successfully obtained with good colloidal stability for more than six months, whereas in the absence of BA (Far100), the latex exhibited low colloidal stability, phase separation, and low monomer conversion (∼30 %). The grafting of BA and Far onto anionic cassava starch was confirmed by FTIR and 13C NMR analysis. The Tg values obtained ranged from −34 to +3.2 °C, depending on the Far content. A decrease in molar mass and an increase in gel content suggest the occurrence of crosslinking reactions. The incorporation of Far decreases the thermal stability of poly(BA-co-Far)-g-ACS and decreases elongation at break. At lower Far contents (≤20 wt%), the hardness and elongation at break decreased. The adhesive properties and peel strength values improved with increasing Far content, reaching their maximum values at 30 wt% of Far. Therefore, incorporating up to 30 wt% of Far into the poly(BA-co-Far)-g-ACS proves to be an effective strategy for adhesive applications. Moreover, optimizing the Far/BA ratio provides a new approach for tailoring end-use properties for specific applications.
